opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing I'd do is be quite careful, maybe even conservative. WeChat is in a very unusual position: it's not just a product, it's closer to infrastructure for people's social lives, payments, and work. So the cost of getting agents wrong is much higher than for a startup. If an agent sends the wrong message to your boss or makes the wrong payment, that breaks trust, and trust is the core asset of WeChat.

So I wouldn't rush to put a big, general "do everything for you" agent in the center of the chat interface. I'd think about where the value of agents actually comes from. My view is that agents create the most value when they have context, and when they connect to an environment where actions are meaningful. WeChat has both, maybe more than almost any other product in the world. It has your relationships, your conversations, mini programs, official accounts, payments. That's an incredibly rich environment.

The question is how to use it without destroying the user experience. I'd probably start from the edges rather than the core. For example, mini programs and services: there are millions of them, and today a user has to find them, open them, and click through forms. An agent that can operate across those services on your behalf, like booking, ordering, or filling out paperwork, is very natural. That's also where the ecosystem benefits, not just WeChat itself.

Second, I'd think about agents as participants rather than as a replacement for the user. In WeChat, the natural unit is the conversation. So maybe an agent is something you can bring into a chat, like a friend or an assistant in a group, that helps coordinate a dinner or summarize what you missed. That fits the existing mental model much better than a separate super-app-inside-the-super-app.

Third, and this is more strategic: I'd think hard about the platform question. Is WeChat going to build the agent, or be the environment where many agents operate? Historically, WeChat's strength has been as a platform with restraint, Allen Zhang's philosophy of not over-optimizing and letting the ecosystem grow. I think that philosophy actually maps quite well onto the agent era. Provide the rails: identity, permissions, payments, a way for agents to safely act. Then let lots of people build on top.

And finally, I'd invest a lot in the less glamorous parts: memory, permissioning, letting users see and undo what agents do. In my mind, the bottleneck for agents now is less about model capability and more about whether the product gives the agent the right context and gives the user the right control. If WeChat gets that right, it could be one of the best places in the world for agents to live. But I'd go slowly, because for WeChat the downside of moving too fast is very real.

r001.rationale: The candidate says WeChat should be careful because mistakes could damage user trust and describes its rich ecosystem, but it does not argue that its defensible incumbent position reduces the need to adopt agents quickly.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not compare WeChat with a different product or identify a dissimilar product as a greater competitive threat.

r003.rationale: The candidate recommends moving slowly, but does not state that adopting incremental innovations early versus late makes little difference for WeChat.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a fun question, and honestly a hard one, because WeChat is almost the opposite kind of product from what most people think of when they think "AI agent."

Let me start with what WeChat actually is. It's not a tool, it's an environment. It has your social graph, your payments, your mini programs, your official accounts, your location, your daily rhythm. And it works because it is incredibly reliable and incredibly boring in a good way. Nobody wants WeChat to surprise them. So the first thing I would resist is the temptation to drop a chatbot in the middle of it and call that "adopting agents." That's the easy move, and I think it's mostly wrong for this product.

The way I think about agents is: an agent is something that takes actions in an environment over time, gets feedback, and improves. So the question for WeChat isn't "where do we put the chat box." The question is "what is the environment, what are the actions, and what is the feedback signal." And WeChat already has the richest action space of any consumer app in the world. Pay this person. Open this mini program. Book this. Order that. Forward this to that group. Those are all actions with real consequences and real feedback. That's the asset.

So concretely, I'd do a few things.

First, I would treat mini programs as the tool layer. There are millions of them, each one is basically an API with a UI on top. If you can expose those as actions an agent can take, you've built the biggest tool ecosystem in the world without writing new tools. Most of the work is standardization, permissioning, and making the interfaces legible to a model. It's unglamorous infrastructure work. But that's where the leverage is.

Second, I would start with tasks that are high frequency, low stakes, and easy to verify. Don't start with "plan my trip." Start with "split this bill across these five people," "pull the address out of this chat and send it to the courier," "summarize what I missed in this 300-message group." These are things where the user can check the result in two seconds. That matters because trust in an agent is built from thousands of small verifiable wins, not one impressive demo. And frankly, the feedback from those small tasks is how the agent gets better. You need that loop.

Third, and this is maybe the most important one, I'd think very carefully about the asymmetry of errors. In most AI products, a bad output is annoying. In WeChat, a bad action can send money to the wrong person or forward a private message to the wrong group. So the design question isn't "how capable can we make it," it's "what level of autonomy does each action deserve." Some things the agent should just do. Some it should propose and you tap to confirm. Some it should never touch. Getting that gradient right is the whole product. The model is almost secondary.

Fourth, I'd be very patient about the social layer. People's instinct is "an agent that replies to messages for me." I think that's one of the last things you should do, not the first. Messaging is about presence. If I know your replies might be generated, something breaks that's very hard to rebuild. So I would keep the agent on the user's side of the screen, helping them act, and stay far away from impersonating them.

And then on the technology side, I'd be honest that current models still have a reliability gap for long-horizon tasks. If a task takes twenty steps and each step is 95 percent reliable, you fail most of the time. So I wouldn't bet the product on long autonomous chains yet. I'd bet it on short chains with great tools and great confirmation UX, and I'd design the system so that as models get better, you can simply dial up autonomy without redesigning everything.

If I had to compress all of that: WeChat shouldn't try to add an AI product. It should become the environment where agents are most useful, because it already has the actions and the feedback that everyone else is trying to build from scratch. The hard part isn't the model. It's deciding, action by action, how much you trust it. That's a product and organizational question more than a research question, and I think the companies that get that right will win, even if they're not the ones with the best model.

r001.rationale: The response describes WeChat’s existing action ecosystem and recommends patience for some agent features, but does not argue that its incumbent position reduces the need to adopt agents quickly.

r002.rationale: It does not compare threats from products that are different from WeChat with threats from similar products.

r003.rationale: It does not say that adopting incremental innovations early or late makes little difference for WeChat.

astra-6.text:
如果我是微信的负责人，我可能会先想：Agent 到底是在帮用户完成什么事情？我不会一上来就把微信改成一个聊天机器人，因为微信本身已经是一个非常成熟的沟通工具了，再加一个能聊天的入口，未必能带来多大价值。

我会先从具体的、结果容易验证的场景做起。比如朋友在群里讨论周末聚餐，现在大家要来回确认时间、找餐厅、看位置。Agent 可以先帮忙整理大家明确表达过的要求，给出几个选择。等大家确认以后，再去执行订位。这中间最重要的不是它说得多像人，而是它能不能把事情办好，以及什么时候应该停下来让人确认。

微信有意思的地方在于，它连接了人与人，也连接了很多服务。小程序、公众号、支付，这些东西已经存在了。我的一个思路是，让 Agent 能够调用这些服务，让用户少做一些在不同页面之间来回切换的工作。当然，涉及付款、发消息，或者读取聊天记录，权限边界都要非常清楚。你允许它帮你订一次餐厅，不代表你允许它随便看所有的聊天。

所以我可能会从一个很窄的场景开始，把成功率和用户信任做出来，再逐渐开放给开发者。最后微信的角色未必是做出一个无所不能的 Agent，而是提供一个环境，让不同的 Agent 能够安全、可靠地替用户做事。这里最值得观察的指标，是用户是不是真的省了时间、完成了事情，而不是和 AI 多聊了多少轮。

r001.rationale: The response says WeChat is already a mature communication tool and recommends starting with narrow use cases, but it does not argue that WeChat’s incumbent position reduces the need to adopt agents quickly.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare threats from products similar to or different from WeChat.

r003.rationale: The response does not state that adopting incremental innovations early or late makes little difference for WeChat.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d start by asking where an agent fits into the relationships and activities already happening on WeChat. I wouldn’t assume the answer is to put a chatbot at the top of the app. People open WeChat to talk to someone, organize something, or get something done. An agent should help with those intentions.

For example, a group chat might be planning dinner. Today, people discuss restaurants, compare availability, make a reservation, and split the bill across several steps. An agent could help coordinate that process. But there’s an important distinction between reading a conversation, proposing an action, and actually taking that action. Those should have different permission boundaries. Being in a group shouldn’t automatically give an agent access to everyone’s information or the right to speak for them.

I’d probably begin on the business side, with fairly bounded tasks: answering questions about a service, helping someone book an appointment, or checking an order. You can tell whether the task succeeded, and you can make the handoff to a person clear. That gives you a way to learn before introducing something much more open-ended.

Then I’d think about WeChat as a platform for agents. What identity does an agent have? What services can it access? How does a user authorize it, and how do they revoke that authorization? Those foundations may matter more than having the smartest assistant on day one.

The metric I’d care about is whether people accomplish something with less effort. If an agent sends more messages but creates more work for everyone, that’s a failure. In a communication product, knowing when to stay quiet is part of being useful.

r001.rationale: The response recommends starting with bounded agent tasks, but it does not say WeChat’s incumbent position reduces the need to adopt agents quickly.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare threats from products similar to WeChat versus products very different from it.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss whether adopting incremental innovations early or late makes little difference for WeChat.
